summary: Redwood SE and AE walked Triton's engineering team through an end-to-end investigation of tail latency. Focus areas: p95/p99 behavior for streaming and non-streaming workloads, network hop contributions (VPC peering and on-prem firewalls), KV cache hit/miss impact, batching windows, and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: run benchmarks using Triton's traces, share security docs, and schedule a canary deployment walkthrough.
transcript:
[00:00] Lina (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We have Marco from Redwood SE who will drive the deep dive. Quick intro round?
[00:12] Emily (CTO): Emily Chen here, CTO at Triton. We own the production ML stack.
[00:18] Ravi (Lead ML Eng): Ravi Patel, lead of infra and inference.
[00:22] Sofia (Infra): Sofia Torres, infra engineer.
[00:25] Marco (SE): Marco Ruiz, I work on runtime and performance at Redwood.
[00:30] Lina (AE): Agenda—p95/p99, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache, batching, quant, and VPC/onprem network stuff.
[00:45] Marco (SE): Quick framing: p95 is often okay, but p99—tail—drives user experience. We'll show what contributes to that tail: queuing, kernel stalls, cache misses, and network hops.
[01:12] Ravi: For us the pain is chat streaming. If streaming stutters at p99 users see tokens drop. We also have onprem gating that might add jitter.
[01:30] Marco (SE): Right, streaming changes the unit of observation—token-level tail vs request-level. Streaming keeps the connection open and flushes partial tokens, so if any hop adds jitter you see token inter-arrival spikes.
[02:10] Marco (SE): First, baseline. We ran your short sample traces (thanks Emily) with Redwood hosted endpoints on a V100-ish sim, and the 95th was ~120ms per response, the 99th was 420-520ms depending on sequence length and KV hits. These are synthetic numbers—we'll rerun with your full traces.
[02:45] Emily: 420ms p99 is... borderline for us if streaming per token. How much of that is network vs kernel execution?
[03:02] Marco (SE): From profiling: roughly 30-50% of tail delay often comes from network variability—VPC peering, NAT, or onprem firewall egress. Kernel stalls and KV cache cold misses are the other big chunk. For very long seq lengths (2k+) the kernel scheduling overhead bumps p99 a lot.
[03:35] Sofia: Our onprem setup has strict egress through a transer appliance; we suspect occasional packet batching there.
[03:48] Marco (SE): That matches what we see. A single extra network hop adding 10-40ms jitter can compound across the streaming lifecycle.
[04:10] Marco (SE): Let's talk KV cache. If you have high prefix reuse—same user context or system prompts—the KV cache hits reduce the per-token compute drastically. p95 improves a lot; p99 benefits too but is sensitive to eviction/TTL policies.
[04:42] Ravi: Our cache hit ratio varies by product; support chat is high reuse but open-ended generator sessions are low.
[04:55] Marco (SE): For mixed workloads we recommend: aggressive short-term TTL for session-level shared contexts, and a staged cache for long-tail contexts; Redwood's runtime can shard the KV cache and keep hot prefixes sticky. That reduces compute-attempts in the tail.
[05:30] Marco (SE): Batching: you want to balance throughput vs latency. Small batch sizes (N=1-4) give lowest median latency but hurt throughput. Adaptive batching windows—e.g., hold 2-6ms to wait for coalesced requests—can reduce p95 without ballooning p50. But for streaming, batching must preserve early token flush semantics; you can't add 50ms per token.
[06:05] Emily: So what's the typical batching window you recommend for a chat app?
[06:12] Marco (SE): For chat streaming, we often use <5ms hold with priority lanes for low-latency users. For non-streaming completions you can afford 10-20ms holds. It's workload-dependent.
[06:35] Lina (AE): Can you talk about quantization impact on latency and tail?
[06:40] Marco (SE): Sure—quantizing to 8-bit gives ~1.2-1.6x perf improvement; p99 drops proportionally but you may see tail variance due to kernel dispatch differences. 4-bit quant (act/weight) gives larger gains but increases potential for kernel fallback, and sometimes numeric instability causes retries or longer schedules if we do dynamic dequant steps. Those translate into sporadic p99 spikes.
[07:20] Ravi: Risk of output quality regression is also a concern.
[07:25] Marco (SE): Agreed—recommend A/B with eval prompts and monitor generation divergence metrics. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per model and run regression alerts if quality drops beyond thresholds.
[07:48] Sofia: Back to network hops: if we do VPC peering vs private link, which is better for tail?
[07:56] Marco (SE): PrivateLink or direct connect often reduces public internet jitter; VPC peering is fine inside same region but cross-account/bounded architectures sometimes route through extra hop. For onprem with strict egress, bring a small dedicated NAT gateway with route rules to avoid shared NATs that can cause queuing.
[08:30] Marco (SE): Also consider TCP tuning, keepalive, and small MTU mismatches—these small items can show up in the tail when connections are long-lived like in streaming.
[08:50] Emily: For security, we need KMS on customer side. Does Redwood support HSM-backed keys and envelope encryption?
[08:58] Lina (AE): Yes, we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations for Private deployments; we'll share the security pack.
[09:10] Marco (SE): On private/onprem deployments latency is often lower if compute is local to the requester, but you trade off orchestration and maintenance. We saw customers with strict residency run Redwood Private inside their VPC and get consistent p95/p99 improvements because network variance is minimized.
[09:40] Ravi: Curious about preemptible GPUs—does that affect tail when autoscaling?
[09:47] Marco (SE): Preemptibles can cause transient increases if jobs are moved; Redwood's serving runtime tries to gracefully move KV cache or warm kernels, but you can see short-lived p99 spikes during scale events. For strict SLOs we recommend reserved capacity or dedicated pools.
[10:15] Marco (SE): Next—streaming vs non-streaming comparison with a simple example.
[10:22] Marco (SE): Non-streaming: request arrives, full generation completes, returned in one response. Latency measured per request; p99 includes total generation time. Streaming: tokens are emitted incrementally; p99 token spacing matters. A 200ms p99 per-token jitter might make a real-time typing experience feel laggy even if end-to-end is within SLO.
[11:00] Ravi: Do you have instrumentation we can plug in to separate network vs compute contributions?
[11:06] Marco (SE): Yes—we emit trace spans across client, load balancer, edge, runtime kernel, and model execution. We recommend enabling token-level traces in a pilot to attribute p99 fractions. We'll supply the tracing config.
[11:28] Emily: Are there known kernel-level hotspots?
[11:32] Marco (SE): For attention-heavy models the softmax and rotary ops are hotspots. For KV cache heavy workloads memory bandwidth and NVMe latency (when spilling) show up. Also watch for GPU kernel launch jitter if the driver or CUDA context is stressed.
[12:00] [12:30] Marco (SE): Quick detour: streaming recovery—if a token fails or we detect a stall we have a graceful fallback to a non-streaming completion for that request. It costs tokens but avoids a frozen UI. Many customers prefer that default for sessions with tight UX expectations.
[12:50] Sofia: If fallback increases tokens, costs go up—how does Redwood report that?
[12:56] Lina (AE): Console shows token-level cost with per-route breakdown and flags for fallbacks. You can set alerting on fallback rates.
[13:20] Marco (SE): Let's talk numbers—example from a customer: normal p50 token latency 10-12ms, p95 18ms, p99 60-80ms. After KV tuning and moving to Private, p99 dropped to 35-40ms. Network contribution went from ~30ms to ~8ms.
[14:00] Ravi: That's the kind of improvement we want. For our heavier models (30B) what's realistic on p99?
[14:08] Marco (SE): With quantization + KV cache + dedicated GPUs we see p99 in the 150-300ms range for medium tokens on 30B; without quant and on shared infra it's commonly 400-700ms. Again depends on sequence length and batching.
[14:45] Emily: Any quick wins we can do while we plan a pilot?
[14:50] Marco (SE): Yes—1) Increase session-level KV TTL to boost cache hits for chat, 2) introduce an adaptive small batching window for non-critical routes, 3) route streaming through a lower-latency path (direct connect/privatelink). We'll run a small A/B for these.
[15:15] Marco (SE): Now I'm going to sketch an experiment pipeline: capture 24h of traces, synthesize a replay (preserving inter-arrival and token sizes), run three runs: hosted default, hosted with KV tuning+adaptive batching, private/dedicated with quantization profile. Compare p50/p95/p99 and token jitter for streaming.
[15:45] Emily: That replay approach sounds right. We can sanitize traces and share.
[16:00] Marco (SE): Great—some extra technical notes: when quantizing, prefer static quant kernels that avoid per-batch recompilation; dynamic quant can cause kernel dispatch variance. Also pin CPUs for the host process to avoid context switching during kernel launch.
[16:30] Ravi: For VPC peering, if we set up peering in same AZ vs cross-AZ should we expect major differences?
[16:36] Marco (SE): Same AZ peering reduces cross-AZ egress and may shave off 5-20ms median and reduce variance. Cross-AZ introduces an extra network hop and jitter.
[17:00] Sofia: Any recommendations for monitoring thresholds? For us p99 of tokens >200ms is unacceptable.
[17:07] Marco (SE): Set immediate alerts on token jitter percentile increases and on fallback rate >0.5%. Also alert on sudden KV hit-rate drops. Redwood Console has dashboards and can export to your Datadog.
[17:30] Lina (AE): Competitor question—how do we handle higher p99 than OpenAI or Anthropic?
[17:36] Marco (SE): Their hosted infra is highly optimized but opaque; we differentiate on dedicated/private deployments and tuning knobs (batching, KV policies, quant profiles). For customers that need strict SLOs, dedicated pools and onprem reduce tail sources.
[18:00] Marco (SE): Let's go into a sample p99 trace we collected from your sample. 
[18:08] Marco (SE): [plays example] You can see a 48ms network spike at t+120ms followed by a kernel fallback at t+170ms — combined caused the p99 ~520ms for that request.
[18:40] Ravi: Can we get those trace exports?
[18:44] Marco (SE): Yes, we'll include the trace samples.
[19:00] Emily: Tuning question—should we prioritize KV cache changes vs network path changes?
[19:07] Marco (SE): Low-effort high impact is KV tuning for chat flows; network changes (direct connect) require infra work but yield stable long-term reduction. Do both in parallel.
[19:30] Marco (SE): On batching windows—we can implement priority lanes so interactive sessions bypass the hold window, but long-running bulk requests join batching lanes. That isolates tail for interactive users.
[20:00] Jordan (Product): From a product POV we care about perceived latency. Are there UX approaches to hide small token jitter?
[20:06] Marco (SE): Pre-fetching common prompts and sending interim filler tokens can smooth perceived typing. But be careful—pre-fetch uses tokens. Consider graceful token smoothing in the client.
[20:35] Emily: On metrics—what exactly should we look at for p99 attention?
[20:40] Marco (SE): Token inter-arrival histograms, kernel launch latency, NVMe spill events, and network hop latencies. Also track fallback counts and retry rates.
[21:00] Marco (SE): We'll also include quantization runbooks—recommended models, acceptable eval thresholds, and per-model kernel flags.
[21:25] Emily: In terms of timeline, we'd like a pilot in two weeks.
[21:30] Lina (AE): We'll aim to start pilot the week of Jan 18th pending the benchmark results.
[21:40] Marco (SE): Any other blockers?
[21:44] Sofia: Firewall approvals for VPC peering.
[21:47] Lina (AE): We'll send the exact firewall rules.
[22:00] Marco (SE): One more technical note—KV cache eviction policies: LRU is common but TTL-based with a hot-key tier works best for chat. Also consider bloom filter based negative caches to avoid expensive lookups for never-seen prefixes.
[22:30] Ravi: Interesting—never heard of negative caches before.
[22:33] Marco (SE): It's a small bloom filter to short-circuit cache misses and avoid downstream KV-store IOPS. Helps tail by reducing miss penalties.
[23:00] Emily: Good. Anything else on the pilot instrumentation?
[23:05] Marco (SE): We'll add token-level trace span tags: network_ms, kernel_ms, kv_hit, batch_size. You can ingest these in your observability.
[23:25] Lina (AE): Recap and next steps—Marco runs benchmarks; Triton shares traces; Lina sends pricing and security docs; schedule canary walkthrough.
[23:40] Emily: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[23:45] Marco (SE): Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[23:50] [END]
